rationale:
Two step-config keys are configured in live agent_definitions and read by nothing, and the mechanism that would have caught them was switched off for both actions. This retires the keys and arms the detector, so the class is caught next time rather than re-derived.

KEY 1 — `commit_from` on update_page_status, 6 live steps (pageflow-builder, page-rebuild, page-rerender, report-builder, section-editor, site-work-orchestrator). UpdatePageStatusAction reads exactly five config keys and this is not one of them. What establishes that is reading the handler end to end, not a grep: it takes `config := params.StepConfig.Config` at v3_site_actions.go:543 and indexes it directly, with no ResolveConfigSetting / GetStringField / GetIntField indirection anywhere in the body and no ExtractActionInputs call, so there is no second access pattern a key could hide behind. It also has no ActionInputSpec today, so no extractor strategy could resolve it either. The value it names (a git commit sha) is never written to any column — the action's UPDATE statements touch build_status, deployed_at, built_from_plan_version and updated_at only.

The reason it looked live for months is the actual finding, and it is why this is worth a council round rather than a silent tidy-up. coordinator.go's prefixConfigStepReferences carried the line `"commit_from", // Used by update_page_status` in its dataRefKeys slice. That comment was FALSE. dataRefKeys is not a statement of what any action consumes — it is a list of keys whose VALUE gets rewritten when a step is expanded inside a loop. Three separate readers took it as a declaration of consumption. A dead key costs nothing; a dead key with a comment vouching for it costs every thread that checks.

KEY 2 — `output_format` on process_approval_decision, 1 live step: simple-content-writer-with-approval.process_approval, which spells the action by its deprecated alias `process_data` (registry.go:1813). Its value is a MAP of four {{.await_human_approval.*}} templates. ProcessApprovalDecisionAction reads exactly one config key, `stop_on_reject` (hitl_actions.go:140), and builds its result from the approval response in CollectedData; extractApprovalResponse takes no config argument. Nothing renders the templates. There is a second, independent reason it could never have worked: the only two readers of an `output_format` key anywhere in the tree (ai_actions.go:1195, database_actions.go:26) both type-assert `.(string)`, so even a mis-routed read would have missed a map. This config has been describing an output shape that has never once been produced.

WHY ARM DETECTION AS WELL AS DELETE. Deleting two keys fixes two keys. The bugs_open/101 machinery already exists to make this class visible — ActionInputSpec.ConfigKeys + CheckConfig, checked by datahelpers.UnknownConfigKeys and reported by validation/workflow.go's checkStepConfigKeys — and neither action had opted in, which is exactly why both keys survived. Opting in is what makes the next one cost a log line instead of an investigation.

WHAT WILL START WARNING, MEASURED RATHER THAN ESTIMATED. A live census of every step using these actions (depth-aware walk, because three of the six are nested in a loop sub_workflow and a top-level `->'workflow'->'steps'` query returns a confident wrong number) gives 10 steps: 9 update_page_status and 1 process_data. After the migration, ONE finding remains standing and it is deliberate — content-reviewer.mark_page_needs_attention carries `notes_field` and `validation_issues_field`, both dead the same way (neither string occurs anywhere in the tree outside an unrelated action's `plan_notes_field`). They are NOT swept into the migration because, unlike commit_from, they encode an author's intent this action has never had — recording WHY a page was flagged — and `pages` has no column for it. Deleting them erases the only record of that intent; implementing them is a behaviour change. So they are left standing and REPORTED, the same treatment migration 350 gave create_work_item's `spec`. That report is the detector working, not a regression to silence.

SCOPE AND WHAT IS NOT HERE. Not StrictConfig on either action — that turns these findings into hard validation errors on live definitions, which is the over-strict-detector failure the ConfigKeys doc comment warns about, and it is the failure mode that would matter fleet-wide. Warn first. No behaviour change to either handler: not one line of executable Go is added or altered, only spec declarations, one deleted comment line, and config removal.

OTHER CONSUMERS, TOLD RATHER THAN MERELY MEASURED (CLAUDE.md owner ruling 2026-07-29 point 3). The shared mechanism touched is UnknownConfigKeys' opt-in set. The consumers are the workflow validator (every message, warn-level, deduped per process) and the offline audit scripts/audit-config-keys.sh, whose coverage numbers will move by three action names. Nothing else reads ListDeclaredConfigKeys. What changes about their guarantee: three more actions move from 'not examined' (checked=false) to 'examined' (checked=true), which is the distinction UnknownConfigKeys' second return value exists to preserve.

COUNCIL: this is presented as a normal gate submission, not an RFC. It adds no vocabulary and changes no shared guarantee — it opts three existing action names into an existing opt-in mechanism, which is what that mechanism is for. The judgement worth challenging is the one about notes_field/validation_issues_field: leaving a known-dead key standing so the detector reports it, rather than deleting it.

plan.summary: Two dead step-config keys (`commit_from` on 6 update_page_status steps, `output_format` on 1 process_approval_decision step) are removed from live config and from the repo seeds, and both actions are opted into unknown-config-key detection so the class is reported rather than re-derived. The false coordinator.go comment that made `commit_from` look live is deleted. No handler behaviour changes.

edits.rationale: update_page_status has no ActionInputSpec at all today, which is why a dead key survived on six live steps. ConfigKeys is derived by reading the handler body key by key, each annotated with the line it is read at, and CheckConfig turns the check on. No Required/Optional entries: this action never calls ExtractActionInputs, so the whole contract is ConfigKeys. Framework keys (input_fields, next_step, timeout_seconds, loop_*) are deliberately NOT listed — IsFrameworkStepConfigKey recognises them centrally and listing one would misstate whose contract it is.

Opts the HITL approval action in. Registered under BOTH the canonical name and the deprecated `process_data` alias, and that is load-bearing rather than tidiness: UnknownConfigKeys looks the spec up by the action string the STEP carries, and the only live consumer carries `process_data`. Registering the canonical name alone would have opted in exactly zero live steps - a silent no-op wearing the shape of a fix, which is the failure this check exists to make impossible.

Deletes the false comment line from the dataRefKeys slice. This entry is the reason the key looked live to three separate readers: dataRefKeys lists keys whose VALUE is rewritten during loop expansion, not keys any action consumes, and the comment asserted the opposite. Removing the entry is also correct on its own terms - with commit_from gone from every live step there is no value left to prefix. page_component_id_field keeps its entry and its comment, which is true.

Removes the two dead keys from live agent_definitions. Guarded and idempotent (re-run raises '... already applied ...', which the runner's probe reads to skip rather than halt), snapshots all seven agents first, and states its target list ONCE in a TEMP TABLE that the guard, the removal and the verification all read - so those three cannot drift apart, which is the failure mode when a nested path is spelled out three times in one file. The verify block is DO/RAISE, never bare SELECTs (ON_ERROR_STOP ignores a non-empty result, so a SELECT-based verification cannot stop a COMMIT); it was induced to fail once against the live DB to prove it aborts, and the whole transaction rolled back with zero snapshot rows persisted. NOT APPLIED - left pending for whichever session next runs migrations.
edits.sketch:
CREATE TEMP TABLE _m356_targets (agent_type text, step_label text, cfg_path text[], dead_key text, siblings text[]) ON COMMIT DROP;
-- 7 rows: 6 x commit_from (three of them at NESTED paths inside a loop
-- sub_workflow) + 1 x output_format.

-- GUARD: raises 'already applied' when none present; raises DRIFT when the
-- count is partial, when a target path does not resolve to a config object, or
-- when any row OUTSIDE the target list carries commit_from (the scope claim,
-- re-checked at apply time rather than trusted from the header).

SELECT snapshot_agent('<each of the 7>', '356_retire_dead_config_keys: pre-update');

UPDATE agent_definitions ad
   SET default_config = ad.default_config #- (t.cfg_path || t.dead_key), updated_at = now()
  FROM _m356_targets t
 WHERE ad.type = t.agent_type AND ad.is_active
   AND COALESCE(ad.is_snapshot,false)=false AND ad.deleted_at IS NULL
   AND ad.default_config #> t.cfg_path ? t.dead_key;

-- VERIFY (DO/RAISE): per target, the step config is still an object, the dead
-- key is gone, AND every sibling key survives - so a whole-config clobber
-- cannot pass as a surgical delete. Then fleet-wide: zero commit_from left in
-- any of the four workflow columns, any row state.

edits.rationale: Hand-run sidecar (the UPPERCASE suffix keeps run-migrations.sh from ever auto-applying it). Restores both keys with their exact prior values. It opens by asserting every parent path resolves to an object, because jsonb_set with create_if_missing is a SILENT NO-OP when the parent is absent - a restore that quietly does nothing looks identical to one that worked.
edits.sketch:
DO $$ ... RAISE EXCEPTION '356 ROLLBACK: % target step(s) do not resolve to a config object - the restore would be a silent no-op' ... $$;

UPDATE agent_definitions SET default_config = jsonb_set(default_config,
  '{workflow,steps,build_pages_loop,config,sub_workflow,steps,update_page_status,config,commit_from}',
  '"page_deployed.commit_sha"'::jsonb) WHERE type='pageflow-builder' AND ...;
-- ... one per agent, then the HITL output_format map verbatim, then a
-- DO/RAISE verify that 6 agents carry commit_from again and the HITL key is
-- back as an object.

edits.rationale: The seed is history, but a future reseed would replay the key straight back into live config, so seed and live row must agree. Seven files, not the six live agents: 034_page_rerender_agent.sql seeds page-rerender (one of the six) and was missing from the brief's list, while 033_rerender_pages_action.sql seeds `rerender-pages`, a DIFFERENT and still-active agent whose live row has already drifted and carries no commit_from today - cleaning it stops a reseed introducing the key into an agent that currently does not have it. Files: 026, 033, 034, 039, 043, 045, 209. The HITL output_format has no forward seed at all; it survives only in historical dump files, which are left untouched.
edits.sketch:
Removes the `commit_from` entry from every update_page_status step config. Two shapes needed different handling and both are checked: whole-line removal in pretty-printed JSON (and where the key was LAST in its object, the preceding line's trailing comma is removed too, or the JSON would be invalid), and inline removal inside single-line JSON blobs. 043 is jsonb_build_object rather than a JSON literal and got the same comma treatment.

Verified mechanically rather than by eye: every balanced JSON blob in all seven files was parsed before and after - same blob count in each file, zero `commit_from` remaining, no parse regressions.

grounded_in: coordinator.go dataRefKeys, the false comment this change deletes: `"commit_from",             // Used by update_page_status`. Its own slice header says what the list actually is: 'List of config keys that contain data field references / These might reference substep output fields'.

UpdatePageStatusAction's COMPLETE set of step-config reads, v3_site_actions.go:534-841, obtained by reading the body: `newStatus, ok := config["status"].(string)` (:550); `if pageIDField, ok := config["page_id_field"].(string); ok` (:558); `siteIDField, _ := config["site_id_field"].(string)` (:584); `pageNameField, _ := config["page_name_field"].(string)` (:585); `if field, ok := config["page_component_id_field"].(string); ok` (:799). `commit_from` does not appear. The single StepConfig reference in the whole function is `config := params.StepConfig.Config` (:543), and a scan of :534-841 for ResolveConfigSetting / GetStringField / GetIntField / GetBoolField / ExtractActionInputs returns nothing - so there is no non-index access pattern for a key to hide behind.

ProcessApprovalDecisionAction's complete set of step-config reads, hitl_actions.go: `if stopOnReject, ok := params.StepConfig.Config["stop_on_reject"].(bool); ok && stopOnReject` (:140) - the only one. The other Config references in that file (:29, :33, :42, :182) belong to AwaitApprovalAction and CreateApprovalRequestAction, both of which start above :95.

The value that could never have been read: the live `output_format` on simple-content-writer-with-approval.process_approval is a jsonb OBJECT - `{"content": "{{.generate_draft.result}}", "approved_at": "{{.await_human_approval.timestamp}}", "approved_by": "{{.await_human_approval.approved_by}}", "approval_status": "{{.await_human_approval.approved}}", "approval_comments": "{{.await_human_approval.comments}}"}` - while both readers of that key name in the tree assert `.(string)` (ai_actions.go:1195, database_actions.go:26).

LIVE KEY CENSUS, depth-aware (jsonb_path_query '$.**.steps', because three of the six targets are nested in a loop sub_workflow and a top-level ->'workflow'->'steps' query misses them), over is_active AND NOT is_snapshot AND deleted_at IS NULL. 10 steps: simple-content-writer-with-approval/process_approval [process_data] {input_fields, output_format}; content-reviewer/mark_page_needs_attention {notes_field, page_id_field, status, validation_issues_field}; page-build-handler/update_status {page_name_field, site_id_field, status}; pageflow-builder/update_page_status {commit_from, page_id_field, status}; page-rebuild/update_page_status {commit_from, page_id_field, status}; page-rerender/update_status {commit_from, page_id_field, status}; report-builder/update_status {commit_from, page_id_field, status}; section-editor/update_page_status {commit_from, page_component_id_field, page_id_field, status}; site-work-orchestrator/update_page_status {commit_from, page_id_field, status}; tool-recreation-handler/update_status {page_name_field, site_id_field, status}.

BLINDNESS CHECK on the scope claim - every agent_definitions row, ANY is_active/is_snapshot/deleted_at state, across all four workflow columns (default_config, task_workflow, orchestrator_workflow, orchestration_workflow) whose text contains 'commit_from': exactly 6 rows, all active, all non-snapshot, all non-deleted, all in default_config only. This is what establishes the migration's scope, rather than the census that motivated it.

notes_field / validation_issues_field are dead, established the same way as the others rather than asserted: a tree-wide grep for either string returns only `plan_notes_field` in write_doc_plan_action.go:38,81 - a different key on a different action. `pages` has no column either could be written to.

DETECTOR PROVED TO FIRE, positive and negative controls, run against the real live config shapes before committing: pageflow-builder -> checked=true unknown=[commit_from]; section-editor -> checked=true unknown=[commit_from]; content-reviewer -> checked=true unknown=[notes_field validation_issues_field]; scwwa via the `process_data` alias -> checked=true unknown=[output_format]; page-build-handler and tool-recreation-handler (clean steps) -> checked=true unknown=[]; post-migration shapes -> checked=true unknown=[] for both; NEGATIVE CONTROL, an action that has not opted in (await_approval) with a nonsense key -> checked=false unknown=[]. The alias case is the one that matters: it is the difference between opting in one live step and opting in none.

The verify block was INDUCED TO FAIL once against the live database, to prove a DO/RAISE block can stop a COMMIT where bare SELECTs cannot: running the file with the removal UPDATE stripped gave `ERROR: 356 VERIFY: pageflow-builder.build_pages_loop/update_page_status still carries commit_from` and psql exit 3. The rollback was then confirmed at the data rather than assumed: zero agent_definitions_backup rows tagged '356_retire_dead_config_keys%', still 6 agents carrying commit_from, HITL output_format still present as an object.

TEST NEUTRALITY, isolated rather than inferred. The working tree carries other sessions' WIP in the same package, so the comparison was made between two clean `git archive HEAD` trees differing ONLY in this change's three Go files. Both trees: build clean; every package ok except a single pre-existing failure in discovery_checks, `TestEveryCheckProducedItemTypeIsClassified` (item_type "decision_regression" has no verifier), whose output is byte-identical between them. Note the brief's other expected red, TestEveryActionInputSpecHasARegistryEntry, now PASSES in both trees - another session fixed it in commit a6c0498f2 while this work was in progress, so it is not evidence about this change in either direction.

The migration parses and runs end to end: run-migrations.sh dry run reports `ok 356_retire_dead_config_keys_commit_from_and_hitl_output_format.sql - ran to its own COMMIT without error (everything rolled back)`, and the _ROLLBACK sidecar is correctly classified as a sidecar and never auto-applied.
plan.risks: MEASURED, NOT ESTIMATED - the blast radius question for this change is 'what starts warning', and it was queried rather than argued. (1) Between this commit and the migration being applied, the validator will log an unrecognised-config-key warning for 6 update_page_status steps and 1 process_data step. Warn-level, deduped once per (step, action, keys) per process by warnUnknownConfigKeysOnce, so it cannot scroll a busy lane. Both halves are independent in both directions: the un-rolled binary ignores the keys exactly as the rolled one does, and the migration is safe to apply before or after the roll. (2) After the migration, ONE finding remains by design: content-reviewer.mark_page_needs_attention's notes_field + validation_issues_field. That is the judgement most worth challenging in this submission - the alternative is deleting two keys that record an intent the platform has never implemented. (3) Neither action is StrictConfig, so no unknown key can fail validation on a live definition; an over-strict validator is the considerably worse defect and is explicitly avoided. (4) Not one line of executable Go changes - the Go delta is two spec declarations, two init registrations, and one deleted comment line - so no runtime path moves. (5) The registry-parity test is the one that could have broken, because this adds three ActionInputSpec registrations; all three names already have GlobalActionRegistry entries (registry.go:927, :1807, :1813) and the test passes in the isolated tree. (6) WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK: that ConfigKeys for update_page_status is COMPLETE - it was derived by reading :534-841 rather than grepping, and an omission there would turn a live key into a false warning; and that registering one spec under two action names is the right way to cover a deprecated alias, as opposed to giving `process_data` its own spec value. (7) The migration is NOT APPLIED and is left pending deliberately; run-migrations.sh --apply takes every pending file, so whoever applies it should read the other pending entries first.
